blocks.text: The **patellar tendon** connects the lower edge (inferior pole) of the kneecap to the shin bone (tibial tuberosity). It stores and releases energy in jumping, landing and changes of direction. **Patellar tendinopathy**, often called jumper's knee, is a load-related tendon problem with pain at the lower pole of the kneecap that is closely linked to loading the knee extensor mechanism [Ref - to verify].

It is common in athletes in jumping and running sports such as volleyball, basketball, athletics and football, and it can also affect recreational athletes. It is a load-capacity problem, not a simple inflammation. Scan changes can occur in tendons without symptoms, so scans should be interpreted with the clinical picture [Ref - to verify].

items: Pain at the front of the knee just below the kneecap, localised to the tendon.
Pain starts with load, especially jumping, landing, sprinting, squatting, stairs and sudden changes of direction.
Stiffness at the start of activity, easing with warm-up, then worse the next day.
Pain may persist after activity or after sitting for long periods in later stages.
Tenderness at the lower pole of the patella.

Pain on single-leg hopping or landing shows load sensitivity. Use caution if pain is high.

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Cannot extend the knee or a palpable gap? **Yes:** urgent referral.
Pain localised to the lower pole of the patella, load-related, reproduced by a single-leg decline squat, and no other cause? **Yes:** working diagnosis is patellar tendinopathy.
Diffuse anterior pain and stair or sitting provocation? Use the patellofemoral pain pathway.
Begin load management and a progressive loading program. Adjust for sport timing and season.
If there is no improvement after a full course of consistent loading, review the diagnosis and consider specialist options.

rows: Soft-tissue work for the quadriceps, hamstrings, calf

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and progressive loading. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not claim that manual therapy repairs the tendon or breaks down scar tissue.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** progressive loading of the patellar tendon is first-line. A staged approach is often used: pain relief with isometrics, then building strength with heavy slow resistance, then energy storage (jumping and landing), then sport-specific work [Ref - to verify]. Pain up to about 4 out of 10 during exercise is generally acceptable if it settles within 24 hours and the tendon is not worse the next morning [Ref - to verify].

rows: Isometric knee extension or wall sit with the knee at about 60 degrees
5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day [Ref - to verify]
Leg press, hack squat or squat
3 sets of 15, then reduce to 12, 10, 8 repetitions as load increases; 3 days a week for about 12 weeks [Ref - to verify]
Good control and no next-day flare
Hopping, skipping, pogo jumps, then jumping and landing
Pain stays under about 4 out of 10

blocks.text: **Supporting exercises:** hip and calf strengthening (bridge, calf raise), trunk control, and landing technique practice. Landing mechanics training may reduce load on the tendon, but evidence is limited [Ref - to verify].

**Load management:** reduce, rather than stop, jumping and sprinting load until pain settles. Keep a log of volume, intensity and pain. In-season, isometrics may reduce pain for a short time and allow play, but this effect is temporary [Ref - to verify].

**Return to sport criteria (example):** pain at or below a low level during sport drills, VISA-P improving, good single-leg strength and landing control, and tolerance of jumping volume. No fixed date is given.

rows: Option for persistent pain after several months of loading
May reduce pain during activity; limited evidence [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: **Medical options (decided by doctors):** corticosteroid injection into the tendon is generally avoided because of the rupture risk. Other injections and surgery are for persistent cases after months of non-surgical care [Ref - to verify].

items: **Visit 1:** screen for rupture and other flags, explain tendinopathy as a load problem, set goals and timeline.
**Early:** manage jumping load, begin isometrics if painful.
**Middle:** progress heavy slow resistance and supporting hip and calf strength for about 12 weeks.
**Late:** energy storage and sport-specific loading, planned return to training.
**If no improvement after about 3 to 6 months of consistent loading:** review the diagnosis and consider specialist options.

blocks.text: Record VISA-P, pain on a single-leg decline squat or hop test, tendon palpation response, strength tests, and training load tolerance.

rows: Higher VISA-P, lower pain during sport drills
No improvement after about 12 weeks of consistent loading
Sudden pop or inability to extend the knee

blocks.text: **Case:** A 25-year-old volleyball player has 4 months of pain just below the kneecap that is worse after training and with jumping. The lower pole of the patella is tender. A single-leg decline squat reproduces his pain at the tendon. Strength is good and there is no swelling or locking. He can extend the knee fully against gravity.

**Working diagnosis:** patellar tendinopathy. **Plan:** education, reduce jump volume, isometrics for pain, heavy slow leg press for about 12 weeks, add hip and calf strengthening, then plyometrics and sport drills.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why use a decline squat? The decline position increases tendon load and reduces the contribution of other structures, so it helps reproduce tendon pain.
Why is deep friction not recommended? Evidence does not show lasting benefit, and tendon capacity is built by loading.
The patient says he felt a pop and cannot lift his straight leg. What now? Suspect complete rupture and refer urgently.
Why avoid steroid injection into the tendon? Because of the risk of tendon weakening and rupture [Ref - to verify].

How do you separate patellar tendinopathy from patellofemoral pain? Tendinopathy is a localised point of pain at the lower pole, triggered by jumping and tendon loading, while patellofemoral pain is more diffuse around or behind the kneecap and linked to squats, stairs and sitting.
**Initial approach:** exclude rupture, then education, load management and progressive loading.
**Justifying findings:** localised lower pole pain, decline squat positive, load-related pattern.
**Priority:** tendon capacity and sport readiness.
**Manual therapy:** minor adjunct.
**Exercise:** isometrics, heavy slow resistance, hip and calf strengthening, energy storage, sport drills.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** common and treatable; it takes months; keep training within limits.
**Avoid:** complete rest, steroid injection into the tendon, rushing back to full jumping.
**Measure:** VISA-P, decline squat pain, hop tolerance.
**If no improvement:** specialist review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** sport function restored and maintenance strength plan.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult athlete, no rupture, no systemic cause.

items: **Can be tested:** which loading program works best; whether shockwave or other options add benefit.
**Hypotheses:** that loading improves tendon capacity and neural control of pain.
**Future questions:** best dose and timing, in-season management, and prevention.
